extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, press-release writers, and PR students
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Cutlip & Center's Seven Cs to evaluate or craft press releases so they are newsworthy and easy for editors to use. The checklist assesses source trustworthiness, timing/context, message relevance, clarity, narrative fit, distribution channel, and editorial effort required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication begins in a climate of belief. Does the release come from a source the receiving editor will already trust (track record of accuracy, named expert quote, institutional standing)? Does the sender visibly serve the receiver (editor / public) rather than only the issuer?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show institutional standing, accurate track record, named expert quotes; frame the sender as serving the editor/reader rather than merely promoting the issuer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context
rubrics_metrics.description: The release must square with the realities of its environment. Does the announcement fit the current moment — news cycle, political climate, audience expectations? A release that lands without context is invisible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time the release to the news cycle and audience expectations; ensure the announcement connects to current events or ongoing themes so it isn't treated as irrelevant or mistimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Messages must have meaning and relevance for the receiver. Does the release answer "why does this matter to this audience?" — i.e., is the relevance to the editor's readers explicit?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the benefit or relevance explicit for the target readership; avoid self-referential claims that don't translate into reader value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Words must carry the same meaning for sender and receiver; complex ideas must be distilled. Is jargon translated? Are sentences short, concrete, and scannable in the inverted-pyramid lead?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain language, short concrete sentences, an inverted-pyramid lead; translate or eliminate jargon so editors and readers immediately grasp the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity and Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication is an unending process; repetition with variation is required. Does the release fit a sustained narrative arc the issuer has been developing, or does it appear as a one-off out of nowhere?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position the release within the issuer's ongoing narrative or campaign; ensure messages are consistent with past communications so editors and audiences see coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Established channels the receiver already uses are most effective. Is the release distributed through the wire/embargo/email channel the targeted editor actually monitors, in the format that channel expects?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose distribution methods editors use (wire services, embargo protocols, direct email) and format the release to meet channel expectations and technical requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capability of audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication works best when it requires least effort from the receiver. Has the release pre-formatted quotes, images, statistics, and contact details so an editor can publish with minimal additional work? (This is also Gandy's "information-subsidy" test; see Gandy 1982.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide ready-to-use assets (quote blocks, images, data snippets, clear contact info) so editors can publish quickly with little additional reporting or editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness (earlier mnemonic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier seven-Cs variant: Completeness — ensure necessary information is included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the historical mnemonic emphasizing that a communication should include all essential facts; overlaps with Content and Capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness (earlier mnemonic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier seven-Cs variant: Conciseness — be brief and to the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer brevity and economy of wording so the core message is immediately visible; overlaps with Clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration (earlier mnemonic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier seven-Cs variant: Consideration — take the receiver's perspective into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor tone, content, and format to the needs and expectations of the editor and audience; aligns with Context and Content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concreteness (earlier mnemonic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier seven-Cs variant: Concreteness — use specific, tangible details rather than vague language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concrete facts, examples, and numbers to make claims verifiable and useful for editors; supports Clarity and Credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtesy (earlier mnemonic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier seven-Cs variant: Courtesy — maintain respectful and professional tone toward recipients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a polite, professional voice and respect editorial constraints; helps maintain long-term Credibility and Channels effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness (earlier mnemonic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier seven-Cs variant: Clearness — ensure the message is understandable (overlaps with Clarity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguity and confusing phrasing; make the main point explicit in the lead and headline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness (earlier mnemonic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier seven-Cs variant: Correctness — factual and grammatical accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure facts, figures, names, and grammar are accurate; errors undermine Credibility and pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use as a rubric / scoring guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: A high-pickup release scores positively on all seven; weakness on any single C — most commonly Context (mistimed) or Capability (asks editor to do too much work) — is a typical failure mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess all seven Cs when predicting pickup: a single major deficiency can sink a release. Pay special attention to timing/context and the editor's required effort (capability/information-subsidy).
